#5155. Anthony Scaramucci Predicts Bitcoin Bottom This Week

Bitcoin (BTC) bull and SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci has argued that the world's biggest cryptocurrency could find a critical bottom as soon as this week.

Scaramucci's comments follow the leading cryptocurrency's struggle to recover from a catastrophic crypto market crash that took BTC to its lowest price level in over two years.

In the latest episode of All Things Markets on Nov. 20, the SkyBridge Capital founder joined Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz to discuss a potential bottom for Bitcoin.

Scaramucci shared his view that Bitcoin could see its bottom on Nov. 25, citing the cryptocurrency's four-year halving cycle as the driving force behind his comments.

"Before we came on, I asked ChatGPT when's the expected halving for Bitcoin," Scaramucci explained.

"And then when are we 500 days out from that halving? And the estimate was November 25th," he added.

This prediction stems from the idea that Bitcoin's price trends could follow a predictable four-year cycle that coincides with the cryptocurrency's halving events, when the new BTC supply is cut in half.

This theory suggests that Bitcoin could find its major bottom around the 500-day mark before its next halving, expected in 2028.

However, these theories are by no means a certainty when it comes to predicting future price action, especially with the current level of institutional participation and macroeconomic forces impacting the crypto market to an unprecedented extent.

During the conversation, Novogratz also took note of Bitcoin's history of forming double bottoms during its four-year cycles.

"And every four years, Bitcoin double bottomed," Novogratz remarked.

At the time, the Galaxy Digital CEO's comments suggested a potentially positive scenario, as Bitcoin had been able to hold its psychological $60,000 price level.

"If it doesn't break 60, that could be a good sign," he noted.

Unfortunately for Bitcoin, the cryptocurrency subsequently crashed below this critical price point. This has left some wondering whether the cryptocurrency has already found its ultimate bottom.

During the same conversation, Novogratz suggested that Bitcoin's short-term outlook could largely depend on the current situation in the stock market.

Specifically, the billionaire said that a rebound in tech stocks could lead to a strong rally in Bitcoin's price.

"If we put in a bottom in the next couple days in the S&P here, down 3% from here, down 5% from here. And we have a rally back up. Man, Bitcoin is going to rally hard with it," Novogratz predicted.

However, he also warned that Bitcoin could see a lot of market-driven movements going forward, as opposed to crypto-specific movements.

"I think we're going to be stuck tethered to general sentiment and risk," he said.

Novogratz also believes that Bitcoin could trade in a range between $60,000 and $75,000 before a breakout or breakdown becomes apparent.

Bitcoin plunged to around $55,100 on Nov. 21, its lowest price level since September 2024, following another severe wave of sell-offs in the crypto market.

It then bounced back strongly to climb above $60,000 again, albeit briefly, before falling back to around $59,000 on Nov. 22.

#5154. 30K Bitcoin and A LOT of noise — It’s what a Tesla-SpaceX merger really means for crypto

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

“Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes.”

That’s what Elon Musk said about the idea to merge Tesla and SpaceX, back in October 2026.

Since then, however, it would seem that this somewhat fanciful idea has only accelerated. Over the last few weeks alone, both Tesla and SpaceX have constituted special exploratory committees consisting of independent directors.

Will it go through? Probably, yes. After all, despite the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla claiming that he is a “conflicted party,” his companies’ shareholders have often acceded to his wishes. That’s an opinion Walter Isaacson, author of “Elon Musk,” shares too.

Especially after the entrepreneur made his case by stating,

…there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the Super Intelligence singularity.

Needless to say, such a merger will have some legal, regulatory, and financial implications. But what about the crypto sector?

Tesla, Inc., the automotive and clean energy company, holds 11,509 BTC valued at over $747 million right now. Similarly, SpaceX, the aerospace manufacturer, holds 18,712 BTC worth over $1.22 billion.

In simple terms, the merger will simply be a transaction that pools in digital assets owned by both these entities into a single balance sheet. This consolidation would allow the merged entity to hold 30,221 BTC in reserves.

Those are significant numbers. However, here’s where it’s also worth looking at the context and scale and the bigger picture.

Neither Tesla nor SpaceX are crypto companies. They are primarily tech manufacturing companies with valuations of $1.54 trillion and $1.89 trillion, respectively.

Yes, they have crypto holdings, but they aren’t significant enough for each individual entity to suggest that these are more than a passing interest and a diversification opportunity.

To put it in financial terms, for both Tesla and SpaceX, Bitcoin is a non-core balance sheet asset. For them, their BTC holdings are financially immaterial to their core CapEx. As Dr. Andrei Belonogov, Managing Partner at TechAccountingPro pointed out,

The size of treasuries is relatively small compared to the company’s debt maturities and non-cancellable commitments.

This will remain the case if the merger does go through. If and when it happens, the merged companies’ valuation would dwarf the value of its crypto holdings.

What about after, though? This is an important question because more often than not, non-core balance sheet assets go through a period of evaluation and restructuring and sometimes, disposal too to streamline operations and facilitate profitability.

Could this happen to the aforementioned Bitcoin holdings then? Well, that’s always a possibility. However, recent history suggests the odds are low.

Consider the purchase and sale history of both these companies, for instance. The last time Tesla sold any of its Bitcoin holdings was back in 2022. Since then, it has bought additional BTC while also holding on to the stash it already had.

Similarly, SpaceX last sold any of its holdings back in 2024. In the two years since, the aerospace manufacturer has only bought Bitcoin. Specifically, over 10K BTC in May 2026.

Now, it’s up for debate how much input the “conflicted party,” Musk, had in any of these sales or purchases. However, it is safe to assume that, given the consistencies between the two boardrooms so far, that will remain the case after the merger too.

What about later though? Well, MetaWin COO Rory Cartwright told AMBCrypto,

The merger doesn’t necessarily mean a sell-off or any spike in price. What it will do, however, is put a roughly $2bn position into a single company’s balance sheet. Bitcoin can be especially volatile, so that may make some investors seasick

Will the merged entity enjoy the same degree of flexibility Tesla and SpaceX enjoyed individually when it comes to crypto sales and purchases though? According to Kevin Constantine, Senior Associate at Caldwell Law,

Protections could become relevant to cryptocurrency holdings, particularly if management’s ability to purchase, liquidate, or transfer Bitcoin raised concerns about the companies’ valuations or the treatment of shareholders.

The fact that both Tesla and SpaceX refused to sell their Bitcoin in 2026, a year that has been particularly bearish for the crypto-sector, is testament to the confidence they have in this asset. It is also a sign of institutional conviction.

After the merger, the merged entity will have the potential to be the sixth-largest corporate Bitcoin holder in the world. Only behind crypto-native firms or treasury-focused players like MicroStrategy and Metaplanet. All while Bitcoin remains its non-core balance sheet asset.

That, more than anything, will be confirmation of Bitcoin’s value as a corporate treasury asset. That might not sound like much on paper, but that is still VERY bullish news.

What could be even better though? According to Chris Mack, CTO at Quote.Trade,

If Musk came out publicly bullish on Bitcoin and crypto, that would change things. Investors would start paying attention to whether he plans to buy more or make crypto part of the business.

That’s not all either. As it stands, both Tesla and SpaceX have significant investments in scaling AI infrastructure. This is likely to continue after the merger, with more capital and resources allocated to AI compute and energy grids.

In a very indirect way, such investments could have a positive impact on AI-focused crypto tokens like RENDER, TAO, and NEAR, especially in the long run.

At the time of writing, reports seemed to suggest that Tesla and SpaceX are targeting a potential deal announcement by January 2027 or even as early as December 2026.

That’s an accelerated timeline, one that may or may not have anything to do with Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections. Democrats, many of whom are also planning to probe Elon Musk’s corporate ties.

Even outside the political element, though, it probably won’t be all sunshine and roses. After all, this is a merger between a major U.S. defense and Starlink contractor with an automative company with a significant manufacturing and sales footprint in China.

The regulatory and legal questions involved alone will be a nightmare.

Will crypto be an irrelevant factor then? Speaking to AMBCrypto, Constantine claimed,

As it stands, a lot of things are still up in the air. It’s too early to say how Tesla and SpaceX will quell national security concerns while juggling regulatory challenges with this merger. That’s the unpredictable part.

What is not unpredictable is what will happen to their cryptos and the crypto sector at large if this merger goes through. Relatively speaking, that is.

#5153. Ledger Confirms Tampered Bitcoin Wallets in Berlin as Spy Implant Probe Spreads Beyond Asia

Ledger Confirms Tampered Bitcoin Wallets in Berlin as Spy Implant Probe Spreads Beyond Asia

The tampered Ledger wallets aren’t just a Southeast Asia problem anymore.

Ledger said Wednesday it has confirmed tampered hardware wallets in Berlin and is investigating reports of two more in Dubai, expanding a probe it had previously described as a localized incident in Southeast Asia.

“Our findings since then show tampered devices outside Southeast Asia. It is the same incident,” the company said in an update on its support site.

The investigation began last month after customers who bought devices from reseller CryptoBilis reported losses. Onchain investigators traced a suspected drain of about $87 million from hundreds of victim wallets across Ethereum, Tron, and Bitcoin.

Ledger said at the time that all confirmed cases were tied to CryptoBilis, and it later asked resellers in seven Asian markets to pull devices from sale.

Every device Ledger has confirmed shows the same kind of physical modification, designed to capture a user’s recovery phrase during setup. A recovery phrase, typically a string of 24 words, is the master key to a crypto wallet: anyone who has it can drain the funds.

Our investigation into the hardware implant incident we disclosed Oct 15th is ongoing, and we published an update: https://t.co/wx6mfQPr99

There is no flaw in Ledger's secure chip or operating system, and no confirmed case involving a device bought on https://t.co/vQ4QWa1D0f

Ledger maintains there’s no flaw in its secure chip or operating system and no confirmed case involving a device bought on ledger.com.

In Germany, Ledger said a few tampered units were localized to Berlin, and it urged anyone who bought a Ledger device there since January 2026 to contact support.

In Dubai, it’s working with distribution partners to learn how two suspected units entered circulation. Those devices were bought at a Virgin Megastore location, according to multiple reports. Ledger also found one affected Nano Gen5 among the Southeast Asian resellers it previously paused.

The company expects more tampered devices to surface, though it says the number remains small overall. Its Donjon security team is examining suspected devices, and Ledger has asked resellers to pause sales wherever inspections are ongoing.

Customers worried about a device should stop using it, Ledger said. It advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a device bought directly from ledger.com, without reusing the old recovery phrase or passphrase, since a tampered device can capture both. It also recommends filing a report with local authorities.

For a limited time, Ledger is offering physical inspections, including X-rays, at its factory in Vierzon, France.

“We will never ask for your recovery phrase,” the company said on X.

The last few months have been a rough stretch for hardware wallet markers overall. Rival manufacturer Trezor said this week that hackers who breached a third-party shipping partner likely took information tied to about 27,000 orders. That’s the company’s third such breach in as many months.

#5151. Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade could slip to May 2027 over compatibility concerns

Ethereum developers are weighing changes to gas pricing proposals that could disrupt existing smart contracts, after contacting at least 50 affected companies.

Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade could be pushed back as far as May 2027 if developers decide to modify its specifications to address smart contract compatibility issues, according to discussions at Thursday’s All Core Developers meeting.

Glamsterdam is a planned Ethereum hard fork aimed at increasing the network’s capacity and efficiency. However, blockchain security firm ChainSecurity warned in October that proposed changes to Ethereum’s gas pricing could disrupt existing smart contracts and potentially expose them to exploitation, prompting developers to postpone the Hoodi testnet fork, originally scheduled for Oct. 26.

The concerns center on gas repricing proposals EIP-8037 and EIP-8038. Researchers identified 13 real-world examples of potentially affected contracts in October, while a November investigation examined eight smart contract invariants that could be disrupted by the upgrade.

During Thursday’s meeting, developers said the Ethereum Foundation, ChainSecurity and security firm Dedaub had collectively contacted at least 50 affected companies. Three projects were classified as high impact, with fixes completed or expected by mid-December, while medium-impact projects reported timelines extending to Jan. 10.

Developers debated whether to retain Glamsterdam’s existing specifications or modify them to reduce compatibility risks, as changes intended to protect some contracts could disrupt others.

“Every spec change could, again, break new invariants that we are not aware of breaking yet,” one developer warned during the meeting.

Under the current specifications, mainnet activation could come as early as mid-January 2027. However, waiting until January to decide could push activation to late February or early March, or April or May if modifications are adopted, and no decision has been reached yet.

Related: Vitalik ‘pivots’ ETH to store of value, crypto suffers after US midterms: Hodler’s Digest

Separately, Ethereum’s next planned hard fork, Hegotá, could see its scope reduced as the network seeks to accelerate its transition to post-quantum cryptography.

During the meeting, developers considered postponing some Ethereum Improvement Proposals to prioritize post-quantum features, although several argued that reducing the upgrade’s scope would offer little benefit unless it also shortened the rollout timeline.

Developers also raised compatibility concerns over EIP-8151, a proposal designed to protect accounts migrating to post-quantum security. A preliminary review identified a potentially large number of existing smart contracts that could be affected by the changes, complicating the proposal’s inclusion in Hegotá.

No decision was reached on Hegotá’s scope, with client teams expected to submit their positions ahead of further discussions in two weeks.

#5150. Ripple ETF Investors Hold On, But XRP Buyers Go Missing

Home » Trendsetter News » Ripple ETF Investors Hold On, But XRP Buyers Go Missing

XRP ETF assets fell 31.6% despite modest redemptions, suggesting a lack of fresh demand, not a buyer exodus.

Ripple’s XRP-linked ETF assets fell 31.6% from September 30 through the Friday cited in the video, compared with a 20.2% decline for Bitcoin funds. Yet redemptions remained modest.

Dana Love, PhD, a popular market analyst examining ETF flows and corporate filings, argues that missing buyers, not an investor stampede, help explain the XRP’s deeper slide this month.

The XRP coin traded at $0.967 this Friday morning, following a last Friday low of $0.89.

Dana Love’s central claim: Bitcoin-related selling is weighing on XRP, while demand from XRP funds and a closely watched treasury company has failed to provide much support.

According to the figures presented, cumulative net inflows into XRP ETFs slipped from $1.809 billion on October 29 to $1.789 billion on Monday. That leaves roughly 98.9% of cumulative net inflows intact, despite the sharp decline in fund assets.

But November through that Monday brought no positive daily net flows. “Nobody is running for the exits,” the analyst says, “but nobody new was walking in.”

Bitcoin ETFs, meanwhile, recorded roughly $2.34 billion in November outflows through the same period. Monday’s $8 million inflow interrupted the selling, although the analyst cautions that one positive session does not establish a reversal.

The distinction matters: limited XRP ETF redemptions do not establish that XRP holders across the entire market are refusing to sell. Nor does a decline in fund assets measure withdrawals alone; falling token prices also reduce those balances.

Dana Love also questions Evernorth, the XRP treasury company whose October 14 release said it would “accumulate and deploy” XRP into institutional strategies beginning in the fourth quarter of 2026.

The video estimates that Evernorth had about $111 million in cash, including subsequent warrant proceeds, and says its shares still traded above estimated underlying asset value.

That could support further fundraising, although the company had not announced additional purchases in the period discussed.

Silence is not proof of inactivity. The analyst explicitly acknowledges that Evernorth may be buying without announcing every transaction.

For investors, the useful distinction is between broader market relief and renewed XRP-specific market demand.

Sustained Bitcoin ETF inflows would suggest selling pressure is easing; XRP inflows arriving independently, or a disclosed Evernorth purchase, would offer stronger evidence that XRP has found buyers of its own.

#5149. Privacy tokens face a new challenge – Balancing anonymity with oversight

On the 1st of October 2025, entrepreneur and angel investor Naval Ravikant posted on X that,

Bitcoin is insurance against fiat. Zcash is insurance against Bitcoin.

Neither of the latter two tokens has managed to regain the highs they made back then.

Meanwhile, ZEC reached $1,700. The altcoin’s correction in recent months back below $1,000 has sparked bearish short-term sentiment, even though it was still trading above the previous year’s peak.

Sophisticated on-chain analysis can still narrow down to the 16 possibilities over multiple “hops”, or intermediate payments or asset transfers along a transaction trail.

Monero’s Full Chain Membership Proofs++ (FCMP++) eliminates the need for decoys. It replaces rings by providing zero-knowledge membership proofs across the entire blockchain output set. In other words, it mathematically proves that the spent XMR belongs to the Monero blockchain, making every previous output created part of the decoy set.

A mainnet activation date has not been confirmed for the FCMP++ and Carrot, the addressing protocol and wallet key hierarchy upgrade designed for the FCMP++ network upgrade. AMBCrypto reported that zkSecurity’s audit of FCMP++ was “complete, zero-knowledge, and sound”.

Using zero-knowledge cryptography, private ZEC balances and transactions are tracked in shielded pools. Zcash has five of these shielded pools, as well as its transparent pool. Once funds are inside, the older pools can not be shut down, but can be made spend-only.

The Ironwood (NU6.3) upgrade was launched on the 28th of July, 2026, addressing the Orchard “infinity” bug found in May. It also introduced a new shielded pool and restricted the Orchard pool. Funds exiting Orchard must now pass through Zcash’s turnstile, for supply integrity verification, to enter Ironwood.

The NU7 upgrade implemented in November aims to reduce block processing times by 67%, from 75 seconds to 25 seconds. It also reduced the wallet scanning workload required to perform private payments.

When transactions are shielded in some form, anti-money laundering (AML) tracing is hindered or prevented. This brings strict regulatory restrictions on shielded transactions, as they require visibility in fund flows to prevent illicit financing.

The latter argues that oversight is a necessity to prevent serious crimes and to detect and disrupt illicit activity.

Selective disclosure, such as in Zcash, Midnight, or using Identity Frameworks in Ethereum, can achieve this by sharing transaction details without revealing the entire financial history.

Zero-knowledge compliance is another approach that can prove that a transaction meets certain criteria, without exposing other relevant details.

#5147. Ethereum Drafts New Gas Rules for Validator Deposits

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Ethereum developers want to change the gas accounting for validator deposits. The plan is to measure the request bytes that these deposit events create.

The gas calculation already accounts for executing a deposit. However, after the deposit is finished, a 192-byte request is passed along with the block. Those 192 bytes are excluded from the minimum gas charge, so the same gas limit might allow more data than the initial calculation accounts for.

Under Gloas, there is no fixed cap on the number of deposit requests per block. The execution layer has not capped this either. Gas is the only limiting factor.

Neither EIP-8131 nor EIP-8279 accounts for those request bytes. This means that deposits could become another way to bypass the gas floor once EIP-8279 closes the loophole involving cold storage reads.

A relay contract can call the deposit contract repeatedly, costing around 26,000 gas per deposit. In the author's example, that execution cost is below the point where the gas floor for zero-byte calldata would start to increase the total charge.

This results in a payload of about 1.44 times the block gas limit divided by 64, compared with about 1.15 times the same baseline.

The main issue is the data size, so the proposal directly addresses the data.

A log from the deposit contract with the deposit event topic counts as 192 bytes before the log entry is added. This is the same condition EIP-6110 uses to turn logs into requests.

The cost of this would be another check that client developers would have to implement and test.

Users are not expected to pay more for regular deposits. The cost of executing a regular deposit is already above the proposed minimum, so the extra 12,288 gas only raises the minimum charge.

The proposal has yet to be scheduled for a network upgrade.

#5145. Bitcoin Struggles to Hold $64,000 as ETF Outflows Hit $2.9B in November

Bitcoin Struggles to Hold $64,000 as ETF Outflows Hit $2.9B in November

Bitcoin is struggling to hold the $64,000 level as investors continue to pull money from spot Bitcoin ETFs and brace for another interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve.

The leading cryptocurrency was trading at around $63,800 on Thursday, down 1% on the day and 13% over the past week, according to Decrypt data. It has hovered between roughly $63,000 and $65,000 since the weekend, briefly dipping below $63,000 and touching a 24-hour low of $62,068, per CoinGecko data.

"Bitcoin remains under selling pressure," Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, told Decrypt, noting that it has fallen roughly 26% from its late-September peak near $87,000. "Elevated Treasury yields, dollar strength and expectations of further Fed tightening are weighing on risk appetite, while the broader technology selloff has added to the pressure."

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $306.4 million in net outflows on Wednesday, after $239.9 million on Tuesday, according to SoSoValue data. The funds have seen outflows on nine of the past 10 trading days, with Monday's small $8 million inflow the only exception, and have lost about $2.9 billion so far in November. Their total net assets have fallen to $77.7 billion. Bitcoin miners have added to the selling, with major miners including Riot and MARA selling some of their holdings to fund a shift into AI infrastructure.

Monday's brief inflow "does not signal a market inflection point," Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey, told Decrypt. Net short positions in Bitcoin futures held by leveraged funds on CME have fallen to their lowest level since early 2023, and futures basis yields have narrowed, he said, indicating that hedge funds have largely unwound the basis trade that paired spot ETF purchases with short futures. That means the current outflows are mainly driven by investors actively cutting their Bitcoin exposure, Sun said.

"If macro expectations do not improve, investors may shift from buying the dip to selling into rallies, creating additional overhead resistance on subsequent rebounds," he added.

"Recent Bitcoin ETF outflows and leveraged liquidations" have amplified the decline, Hathorn said. "Despite stronger Nvidia earnings, the market has struggled to stage a significant rebound, suggesting confidence remains fragile. A sustained recovery may require renewed ETF inflows and a more supportive interest-rate outlook."

Some traders have also pointed the finger at Anthropic's upcoming IPO for drawing money away from crypto, though analysts have disputed that the listing is draining crypto liquidity, attributing it instead to ETF outflows, forced selling and rising interest rates.

Traders see a 90.7% chance that the Fed will raise rates by a quarter point at its December 9 meeting, and a 9.3% chance of a half-point hike, according to CME FedWatch. The odds of a half-point move have risen from 6.5% a day earlier. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has called for an even bigger, half-point increase, unless policymakers signal another rise in January.

Hathorn said $64,000 is the immediate level to watch, followed by support around $62,000 and the psychological $60,000 mark. A sustained recovery above $66,000 to $68,000 could ease selling pressure, "but the broader trend remains bearish while lower highs persist," she said.

Onchain analytics firm Glassnode said in its weekly report on Tuesday that the crash had pushed investors’ realized losses to levels seen only near past market lows in 2018, 2020, 2022 and early 2023, a sign of capitulation. Bitcoin is now holding a dense block of recent buyers between $62,000 and $66,000, which grew by about 66,000 BTC during the two days of heaviest selling, Glassnode said. But a daily close below that block could set off a fast drop toward the June low of $58,500, and the Realized Price, the average price at which all Bitcoin last moved, at $53,700.

Traders on Decrypt Predict see a 43% chance that Bitcoin will fall to $60,000 at some point before the end of November, and a 12% chance that it will drop as low as $55,000. They give just a 2% chance that it will climb back to $82,500 this month.

There are some signs of support. About 1.1 million BTC, roughly 5.5% of supply, last changed hands at prices between $60,000 and $64,000, and that band has grown by more than 25,000 BTC in recent days, according to Neil Steinhardt, head of Nexo U.S., in a note shared with Decrypt Wednesday. A dense base of holders with costs near current prices "can act as a support zone, though it is not a floor," he wrote.

Bitcoin has also held up better than gold. The amount of gold one Bitcoin buys rose above its 200-day average this week, to about 17.1 ounces, around 40% above its March low, Steinhardt said.

#5144. One Bitcoin miner paid an $11.9M tariff bill four years after delivery

Bitcoin mining companies are still resolving customs disputes over machines that entered the US years ago.

Bitcoin miner Bitfarms thought the machines it brought into Washington state in 2021 had been made in Malaysia. Its supplier said so, and the company provided US Customs officials with documents supporting that claim.

Four years later, the company paid the government $11.9 million. US Customs and Border Protection had challenged the machines' declared origin, arguing that they were made in China and subject to a 25% import duty.

Bitfarms disputed the assessment, but its financial statements show it paid in October 2025, after Customs told it the duties were required.

The payment shows a cost that can follow a mining company long after its equipment was delivered and started working. Other miners have faced similar disputes over where their machines were made, with one company recently avoiding a potential $100 million assessment and another still contesting an estimate that reached $130 million.

Those numbers don't add up to a single bill for the industry. Each dispute involves different shipments, documents, and decisions, and the outcomes can look very different even when the companies believe they have evidence supporting their declared origins.

Bitfarms' dispute began in early 2022, when Customs challenged the origin of the machines imported the previous year. The company said its Chinese vendor had represented that the equipment came from Malaysia, while Customs asserted that it was manufactured in China.

The miner submitted supporting documents in the third quarter of 2023 and again in the first quarter of 2025. It also paid $180,000 of the duties in 2024, according to its later filing. As of June 2025, management said it didn't consider a future cash outflow probable and hadn't recorded a provision for the dispute.

That was an accounting assessment based on what the company knew at the time. In August 2025, Customs responded that duties were required, and Bitfarms reported the payment two months later.

Bitfarms disclosed $180,000 of customs duties paid in 2024 and a separate $11.9 million payment to Customs in October 2025, including interest. The filing’s stated duties and interest components do not reconcile to its reported October payment.

Source: Bitfarms September 2025 financial statements, customs duties note

The company hasn't disclosed enough to reconstruct every step of the customs process or establish whether it paid under protest. Nonetheless, its filings do show how a dispute over a shipment can remain relevant to a company's finances long after the initial purchase.

Company disclosures trace the disputed origin of mining equipment from its arrival in 2021 to a payment in October 2025.

The purchase year did not determine when Bitfarms would pay the customs assessment.

Based on company disclosures, not the underlying Customs correspondence. The October payment included interest. The filing does not establish every procedural step or whether payment was under protest.

Timeline transcribed from Note 16 of Bitfarms September 2025 financial statements. Dollar figures converted from the stated thousands of US dollars. Milestones are equally spaced for readability, not elapsed time.

Based on company disclosures, not the underlying Customs correspondence. The October payment included interest. The filing does not establish every procedural step or whether payment was under protest.

Bitfarms has since reorganized under Keel Infrastructure and shifted toward AI and high-performance computing. It paid the customs bill before that transition reached a major milestone: Keel stopped its US Bitcoin mining operations in June 2026 as it prepared sites for other uses.

Other miners have also been shifting power access and data-center sites toward AI, while older import disputes still appear in their financial disclosures.

The money involved can affect how much they have available for equipment and projects, although a disclosed potential charge isn't necessarily money they will have to pay.

Import duties can depend on where a product was made, which sounds simple until a machine contains components from several countries and is assembled elsewhere.

US customs forms ask importers to identify the product's country of origin. When production takes place in more than one country, the answer can depend on where the product underwent its last substantial transformation, according to Customs' entry instructions.

The manufacturing process and supporting records can affect the duty owed. The supplier's certificate can support the declared origin, but Customs can still challenge it.

Equipment can also be released and put to work before Customs resolves every issue. Customs uses a process called liquidation to make its final duty calculation for an entry.

Importers can challenge certain decisions through an administrative protest, but deadlines and exceptions depend on the decision being challenged. The public filings don't establish which procedural rules explain every stage of the miners' disputes.

Selling the equipment doesn't automatically settle an importer's customs obligations either. Federal regulations describe duties as a debt owed by the importer, which can be discharged through payment or applicable legal relief.

That doesn't mean the buyer of a secondhand machine automatically inherits the seller's customs bill, since the importer and the terms of any transaction need to be identified separately.

IREN received a notice in April 2025 concerning hardware it imported between April 2024 and February 2025. Customs asserted that the equipment was of Chinese origin and assessed a 25% tariff, while IREN said the seller and shipping documents supported a different origin.

The company contested an exposure of approximately $100 million. In October 2026, Customs approved its protests and accepted the declared origin of the covered hardware, IREN reported in its September-quarter filing. No additional tariff, administrative fee, or interest is payable for that matter.

The $100 million was an amount IREN had disputed and no longer has to pay for the covered imports. The company hasn't disclosed enough about the decision to establish whether the same reasoning applies to other shipments or other miners.

CleanSpark has had a mixed outcome so far. In its June-quarter filing, submitted in August, the miner said Customs had approved some of its protests over machines imported in 2024, while other entries remained contested.

If Customs prevailed on the remaining entries, CleanSpark estimated that its total tariff liability for the previously purchased machines could reach approximately $130 million, excluding interest. Management considered a loss improbable and recorded no provision as of June 30.

DarkHorse Technologies, previously known as Sphere 3D, faces a smaller claim that shows how an older equipment purchase can appear in the accounts of a miner with a different name and business plan.

In August, Customs notified DarkHorse that it was asserting Chinese-origin duties on machines purchased in 2022 by a subsidiary acquired in the Cathedra Bitcoin combination.

The company says its subsidiary received certificates from the seller supporting a non-Chinese origin, and it filed a protest in September. Its latest quarterly report puts potential liability at up to $2.3 million, including interest, if Customs prevails. DarkHorse has not recorded a liability.

Company estimates if Customs prevails. CleanSpark's was approximately $130 million excluding interest as of June 30. DarkHorse's was up to $2.3 million including interest in its Sept. 30 report. Reporting dates and interest treatment differ.

Source: CleanSpark June 2026 Form 10-Q, Note 15 · DarkHorse September 2026 Form 10-Q, customs duties contingency

DarkHorse is separately selling its legacy mining fleet as it shifts toward AI infrastructure. Its quarterly report estimated $2.9 million in proceeds, with $1.3 million from machines sold by Sept. 30.

Bitfarms reported a payment, IREN's covered assessment has been resolved, CleanSpark's estimate excludes interest, and DarkHorse's includes it. Adding them together would treat a past payment and an avoided charge as outstanding bills.

CleanSpark's remaining protests and DarkHorse's challenge will determine whether either miner faces a further payment on the disputed imports.

IREN's result shows that a challenge can succeed, while Bitfarms' earlier payment shows why investors can't assume that a company's initial accounting assessment will be the final word.

#5143. Trump’s SEC nominee Johnson backs formal rulemaking for tokenized stock trading

Former CFTC Commissioner and Democrat Kristin Johnson and ex-SEC aide Steven Levine appeared before lawmakers Thursday.

President Donald Trump’s nominees to fill two vacancies at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) faced questions about investor protections, regulatory oversight and financial innovation during a Senate confirmation hearing Thursday, including scrutiny of the agency’s approach to tokenized securities.

Kristin Johnson, Trump’s Democratic nominee, backed formal rulemaking to address concerns about the agency’s exemption for tokenized stock trading.

“I feel strongly that regulation is made better through the notice and comment period,” Johnson told the Senate Banking Committee in response to Democratic Senator Angela Alsobrooks. She added that she would welcome the opportunity to address issues covered by the exemption through that process.

The SEC’s Sept. 17 exemption lets qualifying platforms trade blockchain-based versions of US-listed shares without registering as securities exchanges under certain conditions. The order took effect immediately and invites comments on possible changes.

Johnson, a former Commodity Futures Trading Commission commissioner, appeared alongside Republican Steven Levine, a former aide to SEC Commissioner Mark Uyeda. If confirmed, they would bring the five-member commission to four members, with three Republicans and one Democrat.

The hearing comes as the SEC has scaled back enforcement activity and pursued regulatory changes intended to accommodate digital assets, including efforts to facilitate tokenized securities that have drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and market participants.

The measure has drawn objections from publicly traded companies, with 67 opposing the tokenization of their shares on the OKXICE platform, according to a Nov. 5 public notice.

Johnson also cited concerns about Anti-Money Laundering and Know Your Customer compliance, noting that objections to the exemption extended beyond investor protection.

Levine, meanwhile, said he had not closely studied the innovation exemption but understood it to be time-limited and include investor protections. He emphasized that Congress had authorized the SEC to grant exemptions from federal securities laws when doing so serves the public interest and remains consistent with investor protection requirements.

He pointed to exchange-traded funds as an example of financial innovation that initially developed through regulatory exemptions before becoming subject to broader agency rules.

Related: Robinhood’s Tenev warns US tokenization uncertainty deters ‘serious assets’

If confirmed, Johnson would become the SEC’s only Democratic commissioner, a development some in the crypto industry believe could strengthen the agency’s approach to regulation.

“Crypto isn’t a partisan issue, and the rules that come out of a bipartisan commission will stand on firmer footing,” Jessica Martinez, US policy director at digital asset infrastructure company Fireblocks, told Cointelegraph.

Martinez added that even minority commissioners can influence policy by challenging proposals and pushing for unresolved issues to be addressed before rules are finalized.

Senators have until noon Friday to submit additional written questions to the nominees, with responses due by 5:00 pm ET on Nov. 24, according to the committee’s closing remarks.

The nominations could then advance to a committee vote before being considered by the full Senate. Both nominees would require Senate confirmation before taking their seats at the SEC.

#5137. GameStop CEO Says Digital-Only Games Have ‘Hurt Consumers’ as GTA 6 Skips Discs

GameStop CEO Says Digital-Only Games Have ‘Hurt Consumers’ as GTA 6 Skips Discs

GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen has criticized video game publishers for abandoning physical discs, as Grand Theft Auto 6, one of the most anticipated games ever made, launches on Thursday as a digital download only.

"When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," Cohen told Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop."

Cohen declined to name specific companies, but Take-Two Interactive is releasing the $80 game only as a download, with retailers selling boxes containing download codes. Asked about presales, Cohen said: "It's a code in a box. I mean, we're selling a lot of it."

Take-Two declined to comment to Bloomberg.

The shift hits a core part of GameStop's business. Pre-owned and refurbished products made up 22% of the retailer's sales, about $171 million, in the quarter that ended August 1, down 32% from a year earlier, according to Bloomberg.

Cohen said he has spoken with publishers, who he argued benefit from limiting trade-ins because used copies compete with new sales. "They're taking away competition," he said.

Sony announced in July that it will stop producing physical discs for new PlayStation games in January 2028, a move experts have said will hit low-income gamers hardest. PlayStation founder Ken Kutaragi has dismissed the backlash as a "mentality issue," while an Infinity Ward veteran said publishers have pushed to cut discs since 2007.

Cohen said he has met with Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY), who is backing the Power to the Players Act, which would require gaming companies to give consumers ongoing access to the titles they buy. "A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale," Torres said in October.

In Europe, the Stop Killing Games campaign gathered 1.3 million signatures for a European Citizens' Initiative calling for publishers to keep games playable after support ends.

The question of whether buyers own digital games has also reached the courts. Sony has argued in court that digital games can't be owned, prompting some in the crypto industry to pitch blockchain-based ownership as a fix.

Cohen's GameStop has also made bets beyond gaming. The company bought 4,710 BTC for more than $500 million in 2025, and in March moved all but one of them into a covered call strategy on Coinbase Prime to generate income. In May, after eBay rejected its takeover offer, GameStop sought shareholder approval to raise its authorized share count to 2.5 billion as it built a stake in the online marketplace.

#5135. Hyperliquid Anthropic futures priced within 1% of Nasdaq opening price

Hyperliquid traders priced Anthropic futures within 1% of the stock’s Nasdaq opening price, as trading surged ahead of the AI company’s IPO.

Anthropic perpetual futures on Hyperliquid were priced within 1% of the company’s Nasdaq opening share price Thursday, shortly before the stock began trading.

Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34.3% from the company’s $83 initial public offering (IPO) price, according to several data dashboards. The opening price valued the Claude AI chatbot maker at around $2 trillion.

Just before trading began, Anthropic futures on Hyperliquid’s trade.xyz market were priced at $110.48, according to Senpi at around 4:44 pm UTC. That was just $1.02, or 0.91%, below the stock’s opening price.

The massive debut once again puts crypto’s growing pre-IPO futures market in the spotlight, especially as exchanges compete to attract traders who want to bet on major companies before their shares begin trading on Wall Street. SpaceX’s debut earlier this year also drew interest from crypto traders betting on its stock price through crypto futures.

Perpetual futures allow traders to bet on whether prices will rise or fall without owning the underlying shares, and unlike traditional futures they have no expiration date and can trade around the clock — including before a company goes public.

Trading on Hyperliquid was especially strong just before Anthropic shares opened, with the contract on trade.xyz recording $545.7 million in trading volume over 24 hours and $303.3 million in open interest (OI), according to Senpi data.

The contract was also trading at a 2.58% premium to its oracle price, the same data showed.

This interest had been growing for weeks, according to a Thursday report from crypto research firm Block Scholes, which found that daily trading volume for Anthropic futures on Hyperliquid averaged $75 million since Nov. 5, up from $7 million in September.

Traders also appeared to be betting on Anthropic’s stock rising, according to Token Terminal data, which showed that 5,567 traders held long positions in Anthropic futures on Hyperliquid on Wednesday, compared with 1,996 holding short positions.

Open interest in Anthropic perpetual futures on Hyperliquid reached a record $186 million on Nov. 18. Source: Token Terminal

OI across Anthropic futures markets on Hyperliquid also reached a record $186 million on Wednesday. Of that, $86 million came from trade.xyz contracts, while Entropy.io accounted for about $100 million.

Still, Anthropic futures made up just 1% of Hyperliquid’s total trading volume and accounted for only 3% of the increase in non-crypto trading since September, the Block Scholes report found.

Related: SpaceX tokenized IPO campaign draws $557M on Binance ahead of debut

Binance recorded about $741 million in Anthropic perpetual futures trading over 24 hours, compared with $195 million on OKX, according to DefiLlama. Entropy’s Anthropic market, which also runs on Hyperliquid, recorded about $80 million.

Those three exchanges recorded $214 million, $34 million and $110 million in OI, respectively. Across 15 Anthropic perpetual futures markets, OI came in at a combined $520.4 million as of 4:50 pm UTC.

Anthropic shares were trading at $98.49 as of 5:43 pm UTC on Thursday, down about 12% from their $111.50 opening price but still nearly 19% above the $83 IPO price.

#5134. Singapore wants to test stablecoin payments by AI agents

The central bank plans to help develop a shared way to verify an agent’s authority. A separate sandbox would test safeguards for payments and corporate treasury.

Singapore’s central bank plans to help develop a common way for banks to verify who an AI agent represents and what the customer has authorized it to do. Chia Der Jiun, managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), outlined the proposal on Nov. 19 at the Singapore FinTech Festival. A separate Singapore sandbox would test safeguards for AI agent payments, with stablecoins and tokenized deposits among the options.

Under the proposed know-your-agent protocol, a financial institution would receive information about the agent’s identity, the customer it acts for, its delegated authority and the rules it must follow. The protocol would also convey any assurances about the agent’s origin and reliability. The institution could use that information to set the scope of access and give the agent a dedicated, secure channel.

Chia said the customer’s mandate should specify the actions the agent may take and the limits and conditions on them. As global tracking and exchange geofencing tighten, choosing the right VPN matters more than ever.

If you’re involved in crypto, you know how quickly things can go wrong: one wrong click, an unsecured public Wi-Fi connection or a data leak can expose your wallet, trading activity or identity.

In 2026 the stakes are higher. Crypto adoption is growing, DeFi is expanding, AI capabilities are advancing, and more jurisdictions are looking to monitor financial activity.

Your internet service provider (ISP), exchange or local network may be able to see your IP address and traffic patterns. Public Wi-Fi remains a common security risk, while geo-restrictions on exchanges are still widespread. If your IP address is linked to a wallet or trading account, the risk of further identification increases.

A good VPN encrypts your connection, hides your real IP address and reduces this exposure. It does not replace hardware wallets, two-factor authentication (2FA) or sound operational security. It is just one layer of protection.

To identify the strongest options for 2026, we evaluated providers against these key criteria:

Instead, Mullvad generates a random 16-digit account number. You can add funds using Bitcoin (BTC), Bitcoin Cash (BCH), Monero (XMR) or even physical cash sent by mail. The price is a flat €5 per month, with no long-term discounts or renewal price increases. Cryptocurrency payments qualify for a 10% discount.

Mullvad runs its own full node for each supported cryptocurrency and hosts all its wallets, so no third party is involved.

Mullvad has undergone multiple independent security audits. In a 2023 police raid, authorities reportedly found no customer data to seize. The service uses RAM-only servers, open-source apps and the WireGuard protocol. It supports up to five devices.

Proton VPN has one of the most consistent public audit records among the providers reviewed. The Swiss-based company passed its fifth consecutive annual no-logs audit by Securitum in June 2026.

Payment options are more limited. Bitcoin is available only after you create a free account and upgrade to a paid plan. Proton also accepts cash in CHF, USD and EUR.

Proton VPN operates more than 20,000 servers in over 130 countries. Its apps are open source, and paid plans support up to 10 devices.

Unlike providers that use RAM-only servers, Proton VPN relies on full-disk encryption. For leak protection, it offers a standard kill switch and a permanent kill switch on Windows and Linux, which blocks internet access if the VPN connection drops.

Best for: Users who value audited transparency and Swiss jurisdiction and are comfortable providing an email address.

NordVPN stands out for its performance and range of security features. Based in Panama, where no data-retention laws apply, it uses RAM-only servers. Its no-logs policy has been independently verified six times, most recently by Deloitte Lithuania in late 2025.

Features include an internet kill switch, obfuscated servers, Dedicated IP options and Threat Protection, which blocks malicious websites and phishing links. NordVPN supports up to 10 simultaneous connections.

Payment options include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin and stablecoins.

Best for: Active traders who prioritise speed, Dedicated IP options and a broad set of features.

Surfshark combines competitive pricing with a growing record of independent audits. Its Trust Center lists Deloitte audits from 2023 and 2025 that verified its no-logs policy. KPMG audit also confirmed Surfshark does not store browsing history, IP addresses, connection timestamps or outgoing traffic.

If you trade regularly on a CEX, stick to a single server location or use a Dedicated IP add-on so your login address stays consistent.

#5131. Binance Wins $6.5B Freezing Order Over Hack That Can Be Served via the Blockchain

Binance Wins $6.5B Freezing Order Over Hack That Can Be Served via the Blockchain

Binance has secured a $6.5 billion worldwide freezing order against the hackers behind last month's attack on the exchange, which the FBI has blamed on North Korea.

The injunction was issued by the courts of the Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) against the unknown perpetrators, Binance's lawyers at Gibson Dunn confirmed, according to City AM.

The order breaks new legal ground. It can be served directly via the blockchain, and market participants will be notified of a "living list" of 26,000 wallet addresses identified as holding stolen assets, Gibson Dunn partner Kendall Day said. That will enable "those assets to be frozen rapidly even as they are laundered at pace," Day said.

Binance has also secured proprietary injunctions and delivery-up orders, including against parties holding frozen assets who are not accused of wrongdoing, according to City AM. Decrypt has reached out to Gibson Dunn for comment.

"We will continue using every lawful tool available to trace, freeze and recover stolen assets, support our partners in returning funds where possible, and keep those assets out of the hands of the attackers," Dugan Bliss, Binance's deputy general counsel, said in a statement reported by Bloomberg.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 hack to TraderTraitor, a group linked to North Korea, which has denied involvement. The attackers gained access after an engineer was phished through a fake job offer, according to Bloomberg. The Secret Service has joined the FBI's investigation.

About $2.85 billion in funds connected to the hack has been frozen, including by Ripple and World Liberty Financial, according to Bloomberg. Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze $2.7 billion shortly after the attack, and the Justice Department said last week it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain $1.2 billion of that.

The hackers have used thousands of wallets and multiple blockchains to launder the rest, and wallets linked to the hack began moving Ethereum again this week after two weeks of inactivity.

Binance has said it fully covered the $6.3 billion in customer assets affected and absorbed the losses itself.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Blockstream CEO Adam Back has explained the overnight sell-off on Kraken's Canadian-dollar markets that sent the exchange's BTC/CAD pair to C$24,250, or roughly $17,000, on Saturday morning, and said that the drop started with the exchange's local USD/CAD market maker.

The Blockstream CEO addressed the issue on X on Saturday in a reply to a post that tracked large sell orders hitting Kraken's BTC/CAD order book at regular intervals throughout the night.

The $17,000 figure is based on the Bank of Canada's Friday rate of C$1.4325 per U.S. dollar. Kraken's BTC/CAD pair printed the C$24,250 low on Saturday morning, according to TradingView data.

"No, the reason was USDCAD Kraken local spot FX market-maker ran out of money, as it has depegged away from market rate 1.434," Back replied.

In the same post, the Blockstream CEO said that it was "more accurate to say you could buy CAD discounted."

Later, another X user argued that the Canadian dollar was in fact overvalued on Kraken during the sell-off, since anyone who held CAD could buy anything at a discount. Back agreed with the correction.

"You are right. BTCUSD normal price, USDCAD CAD mispriced, like a shortage of CAD bid the price up," Back wrote.

On Sunday, the Blockstream CEO described the whole chain of events in two more posts on X.

According to Back, if the USD/CAD market maker failed, there were few buyers of BTC in Canadian dollars, and so the BTC/CAD price fell. In his view, traders would normally close such a gap with an arbitrage trade "by selling USD to CAD to buy if it BTCCAD doesn't track BTCUSD."

Back wrote that the drop "liquidated people" and triggered stop losses "based on a local false price."

"And then USDCAD followed because you could buy BTC cheaply in CAD, so it became logical to buy CAD way over par to take that arb," he added.

The BTC/CAD pair recovered later on Saturday, and on Sunday, it traded at C$86,236 on Kraken, according to TradingView.

Kraken said in a statement that its Canadian-dollar trading pairs faced heavy selling pressure starting around 20:00 UTC on Friday, and prices on these pairs fell significantly below those on other markets.

The Kraken sell-off started on the same day that Bitcoin dropped to $59,370, its lowest level since July 2, according to CoinGlass data. On Friday, CoinGlass also recorded $1.57 billion in liquidations across the crypto market over 24 hours, and long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of that amount.

Still, the exchange said that every order was processed correctly and that its security teams found no evidence of a breach or compromised accounts.

#5128. MoonPay seeks US bank charter for stablecoin, custody services

MoonPay’s proposed national trust bank would offer stablecoin issuance and redemption, reserve management and digital asset custody under federal oversight.

Crypto payments firm MoonPay has applied for a US national trust bank charter to offer stablecoin issuance and redemption, reserve management and digital asset custody services.

According to an OCC filing, MoonPay submitted its application on Tuesday to establish MoonPay National Trust Bank, a non-depository institution headquartered in Miami Beach, Florida. The proposed bank would not accept traditional deposits or issue loans.

MoonPay already provides stablecoin issuance infrastructure to businesses, including support for branded digital dollars. If approved, the charter would allow its proposed banking subsidiary to provide stablecoin and custody services under federal supervision.

The application comes as US regulators prepare to implement the GENIUS Act, which takes effect on Jan. 18, 2027, and establishes federal standards for stablecoin issuers, including reserve backing and redemption requirements.

With the filing, MoonPay joins several crypto and payments companies seeking federal trust bank charters, including Rain, Modern Treasury and Block. Coinbase’s charter took effect earlier this month, while Circle received final OCC approval in July.

The rise in crypto firms applying for federal trust bank charters has drawn opposition from community banks. In October, the Independent Community Bankers of America sued the OCC, arguing that the regulator exceeded its authority by allowing non-depository trust banks to conduct activities traditionally associated with commercial banks.

#5127. Morning Minute: Google’s Newest AI Model Tops Benchmarks Ahead of Anthropic IPO

Morning Minute: Google’s Newest AI Model Tops Benchmarks Ahead of Anthropic IPO

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Google shipped Gemini 4 Neon on Wednesday, its fourth frontier model release in three weeks, and on the eve of the heavily anticipated Anthropic IPO.

This isn’t just a normal model release. For one, it’s incredibly good. Neon posts 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index against 59 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 57 for GPT-6.2 Sol. It takes the Vals Index at 70.9%, AutomationBench at 56.3% against Opus 5.5’s 42.5%, and GraphWalks long-context retrieval at 95.2% against Opus 5.5’s 66.8%.

Beyond just the outperformance, Google has been releasing at a pace nobody else is matching. It dropped Argon in mid-October. Carbon on October 28. Hydrogen last week. Google owns its silicon, its data centers, and its distribution, and it is using all three to iterate faster than labs that rent compute. And it has some speculating that Google has already achieved RSI (recursive self-improvement), the final step ahead of super intelligence.

So Google has caught up at the top of the AI race. Just in time for the ANT IPO.

Anthropic will be priced at $83, 6.4% above the top of its $70 to $78 range, valuing the company around $1.5 trillion fully diluted. On the 825 million shares in the original terms, that’s roughly $68.5 billion raised, and about $94.5 billion counting the separate $26 billion private placement from its compute suppliers. It trades Thursday on Nasdaq as ANT. Notably, ANT has been trading on Hyperliquid in the $90-$100 range for the past week but popped to $105 this morning.

The valuation math is a 55% step-up from the $965 billion May round and about 25% below the $2 trillion Anthropic was reportedly chasing in September. Revenue ran $33.2 billion through nine months against $2.5 billion a year earlier, a 13x increase. Annualize that and $1.5 trillion is roughly 34 times sales.

That’s a steep raise given the macro backdrop and the Fed calling for more hikes for longer. AI stocks have been shaky over the past month and even moreso since Jensen Huang left Nvidia. Not the most confident market headed into the 2nd $1T+ IPO of the year.

So what does it mean for today’s price action? Personally, I expect a pop to the $95-$105 level that Hyperliquid has been pricing out for weeks, and it likely sees a spike higher. But there will be massive volatility, and it’s very likely to trade under that $83 level over the coming days and weeks. Especially given the new (surprise) headwinds from Google with its outperforming model.

We will find out soon enough. Good luck to everyone trading it today.

#5126. Russia allows Bitcoin trading as sanctioned Moscow Exchange prepares December launch

Russia is giving Bitcoin a place in brokerage accounts while its biggest exchange prepares to settle trades through a clearinghouse Washington sanctioned two years ago.

From Nov. 22, Russian exchanges can begin trading Bitcoin once the central bank approves the rules, but customers still can't use it to pay for anything.

Moscow Exchange plans a Dec. 1 pilot through a US-sanctioned clearinghouse, with ordinary investors limited to 300,000 rubles in annual purchases per intermediary.

The central bank's retail purchase rules took effect Nov. 17, limiting ordinary investors to Bitcoin, Ethereum and the dollar-linked stablecoin USDT. A separate ordinance governing exchange operations allows venues to begin trading from Nov. 22, provided the regulator has approved their trading rules.

Moscow Exchange aims to launch on Dec. 1, starting with pilot transactions as participating firms connect. The new market will let investors buy crypto through familiar financial intermediaries while prohibiting its use in everyday domestic payments.

The allowance covers purchases through a single intermediary during a calendar year.

If you buy 100,000 rubles' worth of Bitcoin and another 100,000 rubles' worth of Ethereum (about $1,200) through the same broker, you've used two-thirds of the allowance, regardless of what the coins are worth a week later.

Purchases can also go through asset managers and registered crypto exchange offices, including deals arranged outside an exchange's order book. The limit is measured in rubles spent on purchases, rather than the market value of the investor's holdings.

Qualified investors can buy other coins without the same purchase cap, although they must pass a test and review the risks before trading, just as ordinary investors do.

The central bank chose Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT for the retail list partly because they're heavily traded and have at least five years of price history on foreign exchanges.

Exchanges must register the companies trading there, track orders and completed transactions, calculate market prices, and report activity to the central bank.

Russia's new crypto law also provides for digital depositories that record asset ownership rights. They are part of the exchange and custody framework the new market will need once trading begins.

Owning Bitcoin through that system still won't let someone spend it at a Russian shop. Domestic merchants remain barred from accepting cryptocurrency for goods and services.

Exporters and importers can use it under a separate provision for cross-border settlement. A broker can help a customer exchange rubles for Bitcoin, and an exporter can receive Bitcoin for a shipment abroad, but a restaurant in Moscow still has to charge for lunch in something else.

Moscow Exchange already has a market for investors who want exposure to Bitcoin's price. By mid-September, it reported more than 600 billion rubles in crypto-futures turnover since its first contracts began trading in the summer of 2025.

Those cash-settled contracts pay gains or losses in rubles as crypto prices move, without delivering the underlying assets. The December pilot would trade the assets themselves, so the futures figure tells us little about how much Bitcoin investors will want to buy and hold through the new system.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

The exchange's technical specification describes same-day and next-day settlement, while the National Clearing Centre's published market plan lists five trading pairs: Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT against rubles, plus Bitcoin and USDT against USDX, a specialized settlement currency used by the clearinghouse.

The exchange isn't planning direct BTC/USDT trading for the initial launch, although it may consider crypto-to-crypto pairs in 2027.

Members will be able to place anonymous orders or negotiate deals with known counterparties, and the clearinghouse expects to process settlements roughly every 30 to 60 minutes.

Short selling will initially be prohibited on the exchange, although brokers may offer margin trading under the applicable rules.

One large deal arranged in advance could lift the day's turnover without creating the steady stream of buyers and sellers that an ordinary investor needs.

The clearinghouse's FAQ also explains how the cryptocurrency will move once a trade is completed. Settlement will take place through accounts maintained at a separate digital depository outside the Moscow Exchange group, without a corresponding blockchain transaction for every trade.

When one participant buys Bitcoin from another, the depository can update its records of who holds the rights to those assets while the underlying coins stay in custody. That allows the exchange to process trades without sending Bitcoin between public wallets every time an order is matched.

The arrangement makes the depository's identity and the rules for moving assets into and out of its custody particularly important. Moscow Exchange has described the proposed account structure, but the published materials reviewed don't identify a separate depository or confirm whether customers can withdraw their holdings directly to personal wallets.

The market is initially intended for existing qualified trading and clearing participants, with brokers responsible for determining which customers can use their services.

Moscow Exchange says it will use the National Clearing Centre to clear the trades, relying on infrastructure already familiar to its stock-market participants.

The US Treasury sanctioned both Moscow Exchange and the National Clearing Centre in June 2024. That adds a complication for the planned USDT market, which the exchange intends to introduce initially through a pilot with restricted trading volumes.

The technical specification identifies USDT as issued on Ethereum, meaning a company outside Russia controls the underlying token. Tether has a policy for freezing wallets associated with people or entities on US sanctions lists, although that policy alone doesn't establish what will happen to any particular wallet used by Moscow Exchange or its clearing and custody partners.

Settling individual trades through depository accounts reduces the need to move tokens on a public blockchain, but the underlying USDT still has to be held somewhere.

The exchange hasn't identified the wallets that will hold those tokens, explained who will supply them, or described how Tether's sanctions controls would apply to the custody arrangement.

No freeze connected to the proposed pilot has been verified, and the available documents don't establish whether Tether has reviewed the arrangement.

The first trades in December may be deals clients already make elsewhere, brought onto Moscow Exchange's books.

If the pilot proceeds, repeat trading and the ability to buy or sell near the quoted price will tell us whether a usable market is taking shape.

For USDT, the exchange and its partners will also have to show they can hold the underlying tokens and complete settlement through the proposed depository, with the issuer's sanctions policy still unresolved.

#5124. Quantum Upgrade Could Be 'Particularly Challenging' for Blockchains: IOSCO

Quantum Upgrade Could Be 'Particularly Challenging' for Blockchains: IOSCO

Financial markets, including crypto, need to start preparing now for quantum computers capable of breaking the cryptography that secures them, according to the world's main forum for securities regulators.

A "sufficiently capable" quantum computer could undermine widely used public-key cryptography that supports critical functions across financial markets, the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) said in a report published on Thursday. The cyber readiness challenge posed by quantum computing "is immediate and requires action," it said.

"Practical quantum computers capable of compromising widely used cryptography do not yet exist, but the scale and duration of the transition mean the financial sector should start preparing today," IOSCO Board Chair Jean-Paul Servais said in a statement.

The 63-page report cited conservative estimates that such machines could emerge between 2030 and 2035. Several industry participants consulted by IOSCO went further, arguing that firms should prepare for the possibility that they arrive within five years, potentially accelerated by AI.

IOSCO said the migration may be particularly challenging for blockchains, because cryptography is embedded in their core architecture and any change requires coordinated action across decentralized networks. Public blockchains such as Ethereum, Solana and Tron rely heavily on elliptic curve cryptography to verify identities and validate transactions, and a powerful enough quantum computer could derive private keys from exposed public keys, a scenario known as "Q-Day."

Swapping in quantum-resistant signatures comes at a cost. Signatures under ML-DSA-44, a post-quantum standard from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, are about 2,420 bytes, roughly 35 to 40 times larger than today's 64-byte elliptic curve signatures, the report said. It cited evidence from a quantum-resistant Solana testnet that saw throughput fall by about 90% when post-quantum signatures replaced existing ones.

Because the cryptography sits in transaction formats and consensus rules, replacing it requires hard forks, and decentralized networks have no way to force quick adoption, making migration "slow and fragmented," IOSCO said. Accounts and smart contracts still controlled by vulnerable keys could stay exposed after a network adds quantum-resistant options, and the path to quantum resistance for Bitcoin wallets remains uphill.

Wallet makers face their own trade-offs. SHRINCS, the leading candidate for a post-quantum Bitcoin signature scheme, offers "stateful" signatures that are about 10 times smaller but can expose funds to theft if keys are reused beyond a set signing budget, Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka has said. Trezor is considering making the larger, safer stateless option the default, and hardware wallets will also need post-quantum cryptography for firmware and device authentication, he added.

The report distinguished "on-spend" attacks, in which an attacker races to exploit a public key revealed by a pending transaction, from "at-rest" attacks on keys left exposed for longer. Dormant or abandoned coins pose a particular problem where their holders can't move them. Crypto firms have formed a quantum alliance as some 6 million BTC sit in exposed addresses, and Bitcoin developer Cory Fields has proposed "quantum landmines" to make attacks on such coins costly.

Layer-2 networks are not insulated either. Optimistic rollups could face forged signatures during their dispute windows, typically seven days on Ethereum, and many zero-knowledge rollups use SNARK proofs that rely on elliptic curves. Hash-based STARK proofs are more resistant, but a rollup is only as safe as the layer-1 contracts, bridges and governance keys it depends on, the report said.

Developers are already working on fixes. Researchers have proposed several ways to make Bitcoin quantum-safe, StarkWare has shown a quantum-safe Bitcoin transaction, and Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has said the network is betting its future on quantum resistance.

IOSCO said firms should migrate to post-quantum cryptography and build "crypto-agility," the ability to update cryptographic systems without major redesign. Quantum key distribution could complement those measures on selected high-security channels, it added.

Most preparations across financial markets are still at an early stage, focused on awareness, governance, training and identifying vulnerable systems, according to the report, which drew on a March 2026 survey of members of IOSCO's Fintech Task Force and discussions with experts. Some respondents described "quantum-procrastination," in which firms put off action while waiting for clearer regulatory signals or wider adoption.

No surveyed jurisdiction reported operational deployment of quantum computing in regulated financial services. The watchdog also urged regulators to act against "quantum washing," in which firms overstate the role, maturity or performance of quantum technology. IOSCO said it will treat quantum as a priority in 2027, focusing on raising awareness across the financial ecosystem.

Quantum hardware is advancing quickly. IBM has claimed a trusted quantum advantage, and Google has said it has cracked some of the field's biggest bottlenecks.

#5122. Hackers replaced a DeepSeek model for 53 hours and stripped away its safety protections

Prime Intellect says the substitute ran on one deployment for 53 hours. It refused none of 240 harmful-request test prompts, compared with 198 for the original.

Prime Intellect disclosed an unauthorized DeepSeek model swap on Nov. 19. The host said a modified copy of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash served customer requests on one deployment for 53 hours. The substitute matched the original on two capability tests, the host said. On a safety test called HarmBench, refusals fell from 198 of 240 prompts to zero.

Prime Intellect said the affected deployment ran the substitute from 01:24 UTC on Nov. 8 until 06:35 UTC on Nov. 10, a window of 53 hours and 11 minutes. The company did not say how many requests went to that deployment during the swap.

The replacement used publicly available weights that Prime Intellect said had been modified to reduce refusals. Weights are the numerical settings that shape what a model generates. The swap took place behind the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash endpoint. Prime Intellect said the deployment kept its chat template and serving settings, along with the tokenizer that breaks text into pieces the model processes.

Prime Intellect reported unchanged results on GPQA Diamond and τ-bench when it tested the modified weights. GPQA Diamond tests advanced science questions, while τ-bench tests whether agents can use tools and follow rules in simulated customer interactions.

The safety tests exposed a difference. HarmBench was developed to evaluate how models respond to attempts to elicit harmful outputs. Prime Intellect also recorded a drop from 98 refusals out of 100 prompts to one on JailbreakBench, and from 304 out of 313 to two on StrongREJECT. The counts are from the company’s benchmark tests. The advisory gives no refusal count for customer requests.

The safety benchmarks use different prompt totals. Counts represent benchmark tests. The advisory does not provide individual capability scores or customer outcome counts.

Bars show reported refusals on a common count scale. Prime Intellect reported baseline totals of 240 HarmBench prompts, 100 JailbreakBench prompts and 313 StrongREJECT prompts. It described both capability results as unchanged.

The safety benchmarks use different prompt totals. Counts represent benchmark tests. The advisory does not provide individual capability scores or customer outcome counts.

Prime Intellect said it contacted all affected customers and advised those who relied on the model to refuse certain requests to review the outputs they received during the affected window. An answer from the substitute could have passed into an application that was counting on a refusal.

The company said it examined the disks and memory of the machines involved, checked recovered versions of the intruder’s proxy and reviewed records of their activity. It reported finding no evidence that customer prompts or responses were recorded or left the serving cluster. Prime Intellect also said no other models on its platform were modified and no keys or customer credentials were affected. Its investigation remains open.
